newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Measures seen unlikely to perk up Singapore dollar.
newsitem.headline: Measures seen unlikely to perk up Singapore dollar.

text.p: The traditionally stolid Singapore dollar is likely to remain impervious to sharp movements despite newly announced government measures aimed at internationalising the currency, economists said at the weekend.

Singapore's Finance Minister Richard Hu recently raised eyebrows with a comment about the Monetary Authority of Singapore's (MAS) policy to allow a gradual internationalisation of the Singapore dollar.

While the statement was initially seen as signalling a shift in the government's stance of keeping a tight rein on the currency, economists said the new measures outlined by Hu were unlikely to spur a sea change.
"We don't see a sudden opening of the flood gates," said Liew Yin Sze, senior economist at stockbroking firm JM Sassoon.

Hu, speaking at the launch of a regional stock index, said foreign companies meeting certain conditions could now apply to list their shares on the domestic bourse in Singapore dollars and ultimately, to issue Singapore dollar bonds.

"It's very positive, but the exact things he announced are still only a very small crack in what is quite a monolithic holdback," Christopher Chong, research director at Kay Hian James Capel, told Reuters Financial Television (RFTV).

Chong said the requirement that foreign companies seeking a Singapore-dollar listing have over 35 percent of their revenue, profits or expenses attributable to their Singapore operations would pose a significant barrier.
Only a handful of the 40 foreign firms trading on the Stock Exchange of Singapore currently qualify to convert their foreign currency-denominated stocks to Singapore dollars.

Liew noted that the Singapore authorities had already shown a willingness to lift some restrictions by allowing companies investing on the Indonesian island of Batam to borrow funds in Singapore dollars.

He said the new measures were unlikely to have much of an impact on the Singapore dollar. "We don't have such a big bond market here and the amount of equity funds you can raise from the stock market is also quite limited."
But Alex Erskine, regional market strategist at Citibank, told RFTV the measures were likely to put the Singapore dollar back on an appreciation track once they gathered momentum.
Erskine said the currency had already undergone some internationalisation as reflected by the fact that Singapore's foreign exchange reserves had risen so strongly in recent years.

"Singapore has to do this to keep its capital markets relevant when Malaysia and the other regional centres are competing so strongly for some business," he said. He added that the new measures were "one step in the right direction".

In addition to increasing the depth of Singapore's financial markets, an internationalisation of the currency would encourage more local businesses to venture offshore, a move the government has long promoted.
"They've talked all along about Singaporeans being not too adventurous. (Now) they could lend more money in Singapore dollars for them to go overseas," said a treasury manager at a Japanese bank.

Under existing rules, offshore banks can lend a maximum of only Singapore $150 million ($106.4 million). But after the measures were announced, Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong said the government would have to allow more lending in Singapore dollars to meet the objectives of regionalisation.

Although no one expects the MAS, Singapore's de facto central bank, to give up its tight grip on the Singapore dollar, the recent moves are likely to bring an inevitable increase in volatility, economists said.

"They may be willing to accept a slightly higher level of volatility in the Singapore dollar in order to achieve the broader objective of developing Singapore into a top grade financial centre," said Andy Tan, economist and general manager at MMS International.
